item.title: Depositors’ protest turns violent in front of Islami Bank
item.description:
The capital's Motijheel area on Monday turned chaotic over the appointment of a new chairman of Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC.
The police baton-charged and fired tear gas shells to disperse a human chain of the “Conscious Customer Forum” in front of the bank's head office.
Additionally, sound grenades and water cannons were fired to disperse the protesters.
Several people were reportedly injured in the chase and counter-chase. Currently, the police and the protesters are in a face-to-face position in that area.
According to relevant sources, former deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank Khurshid Alam was appointed as the new chairman of Islami Bank on the last working day before the Eid-ul-Azha holiday.
Protesters claimed that they will not allow Khurshid Alam to enter the bank under any circumstances, as he was a “controversial appointment.”
Protesting against this appointment and announcing their intent to prevent his entry, the deposits have been stationed in front of the bank's head office since Monday morning.
By 9:00am Monday, the first working day after the Eid holidays, members of the forum began gathering in front of the Islami Bank Tower in Dilkusha, Motijheel.
When they took up positions there and started forming a human chain, the police took action against them. Tear gas and sound grenades were fired at the protesters, and the police dispersed them using water cannons.
Currently, there is tension in the area, as the police and the customer forum members are still in a face-to-face position to avoid any unpleasant situation.

item.title: CHT Affairs Minister Dipen Dewan resigns
item.description:
Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) Affairs Minister Dipen Dewan has resigned from the Cabinet, citing health reasons.
Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon said Dewan submitted his resignation letter to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, mentioning that his health condition was preventing him from carrying out his official duties properly.
The prime minister accepted his resignation, he added.
Dipen Dewan had been serving as the minister for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs in the government formed after the BNP's landslide victory in the February 12 general election.

item.title: Child rape, murder case: Trial begins against main accused, wife
item.description:
A Dhaka court has framed charges and ordered the commencement of trial against main accused Sohel Rana and his wife Swapna Akhter in a case over the rape and murder of an eight-year-old girl in the capital’s Pallabi area.
Dhaka Metropolitan Child Violence Prevention Tribunal Judge Masrur Salekin passed the order on Monday after a hearing. The court also fixed June 2 for recording witness testimony.
After the charges were read out, both accused pleaded not guilty. Swapna Akhter also denied any involvement in the incident.
Earlier in the day, the accused were brought to court from jail around 7:30am and kept in the custody of the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge’s Court before being produced before the tribunal at 11:10am. The tribunal was later constituted within 15 minutes.
As the accused did not have a lawyer, the Law Ministry appointed Advocate Musa Kalimullah of the Dhaka Bar as state-appointed defence counsel. The hearing was conducted by the public prosecutor on behalf of the state.
On May 24, investigation officer SI Ahiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet against Sohel Rana and Swapna Akhter. The charge sheet was later accepted by Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ashraful Haque, who issued an order to transfer the case to the Child Violence Prevention Tribunal for trial.
On the same day, the tribunal accepted the charge sheet and fixed June 1 for hearing on framing of charges.
According to the case statement, the victim, an eight-year-old Class II student, went missing on May 19 after leaving home around 9:30am. Later, her shoes were found near the accused’s flat. After breaking open the door, family members and locals found the child’s body inside the room.
Police said the victim’s father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station the same day. Swapna Akhter was arrested before the case was filed, while Sohel Rana was later arrested from Fatulla in Narayanganj. He reportedly confessed to the crime in a judicial statement on May 20. Swapna Akhter was subsequently sent to jail.

item.title: Swapon: Zero tolerance for interference in journalists' professional duties
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon on Monday said the government will pursue a "zero tolerance" policy against any form of unethical obstruction or interference in the professional activities of mainstream media personnel, stressing that ensuring a fully independent and transparent media environment remains one of its key objectives.
The minister made the comments while replying to a query from reporters at his office in the Secretariat in Dhaka.
Journalists sought his reaction regarding a recent incident in which mainstream media workers were allegedly subjected to an attack by security guards and cleaners while collecting news at a private institution, and demanded justice and protection for media professionals.
Swapon said: "I am gathering more detailed information about the incident. However, it is clear that the professional safety of journalists was not ensured within the concerned institution."
He added: "The primary responsibility of the media is to present all sectors of society transparently before the people. Assisting mainstream journalists in carrying out this responsibility is the duty of both the state and society."
Praising the professionalism of television journalists in particular, Zahir Uddin Swapon said: "There is no scope for distorting information in television journalism as they broadcast live. Our prime minister has repeatedly spoken about establishing a culture of accountability. We will assess and evaluate such undesirable incidents in that light."
The minister said editors, media owners and leaders of journalists' organisations from mainstream news outlets recently met the Prime Minister and expressed satisfaction that they are currently able to carry out their professional duties independently without any form of government control or pressure.
Assuring mainstream journalists, he said that following recent political changes, the new government has had to deal with a large number of cases filed as a result of public anger and protests.
However, he noted that the Prime Minister has given clear instructions that no mainstream journalist should be subjected to harassment or false cases without irrefutable evidence and specific allegations.
"If there is concrete evidence of wrongdoing, the matter will proceed in accordance with the country's existing laws," he added.
The minister expressed deep gratitude to mainstream media organisations for their positive and responsible role during the government's first 100 days in office and extended his sincere greetings and best wishes to media professionals and the people of the country on the occasion of the holy Eid-ul-Azha.

item.title: Joty's valiant 77 goes in vain as Tigresses fall to Dutch upset
item.description:
Bangladesh's struggles in the Women's T20I Tri-Series in Scotland continued as skipper Nigar Sultana Joty's brilliant knock could not prevent an eight-run defeat against the Netherlands at the Grange Cricket Club Ground in Edinburgh on Sunday.
After an eight-wicket loss to hosts Scotland in their opening fixture, the Tigresses were hoping to bounce back but fell short despite a spirited chase led by their captain, who scored a superb 77 off 51 deliveries.
Chasing 163 for victory, Bangladesh endured a shaky start as openers Dilara Akter and Sharmin Akter were dismissed early, leaving the side reeling at 13 for 2 inside the first four overs. With the required rate steadily climbing, Joty walked in and once again shouldered the responsibility of anchoring the innings.
Juairiya Ferdous contributed 22 from 24 balls to help stabilise the innings before departing in the ninth over. From there, Joty took charge, mixing composure with aggression as she reached her 12th T20I half-century in just 39 balls.
However, wickets continued to tumble at the other end, making the task increasingly difficult. Leg-spinner Silver Siegers struck crucial blows in the middle overs, finishing with 2 for 24 to leave Bangladesh needing a late surge.
With 41 runs required from the final three overs, Ritu Moni offered valuable support with a quickfire 17 off 12 deliveries, helping keep Bangladesh's hopes alive. The equation was reduced to 18 runs from the final over, with Joty unbeaten on 73 and still threatening to pull off an unlikely victory.
But Dutch all-rounder Heather Siegers turned the match decisively in her side's favour. She removed Ritu Moni with the first ball of the over before dismissing Joty on the fourth delivery as the Bangladesh captain holed out at long-on after a magnificent innings.
The Netherlands then wrapped up the victory by claiming another wicket off the final ball, restricting Bangladesh to 154 for 8.
Earlier, Bangladesh's bowlers had fought back well after the Netherlands made a strong start. Openers Heather Siegers and Phebe Molkenboer added 57 runs before Rabeya Khan provided the breakthrough by dismissing Molkenboer for 29.
Fariha Trishna was the pick of the Bangladesh bowlers, returning figures of 2 for 26 from her four overs. She removed both Heather Siegers, who top-scored with 52, and Sterre Kalis in the 16th over to halt the Dutch momentum. Rabeya Khan and Marufa Akter also chipped in with a wicket apiece.
Despite those efforts, late hitting from captain Babette de Leede and Robine Rijke helped the Netherlands collect 45 runs from the final four overs to post a challenging 162 for 5.
The result marked the Netherlands women's first-ever T20I victory over Bangladesh, having lost all three previous meetings between the sides.
Bangladesh will now face Scotland on Tuesday, seeking their first win of the tournament and a much-needed boost ahead of the Women's T20 World Cup.

item.title: EC: October-March ideal period to begin local body polls
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) plans to complete the revision and updating of all rules and codes of conduct related to local government elections by June next, considering the period from late October to March as the most suitable time to begin elections to local government bodies.
The commission thinks elections to union parishads and municipalities should be held first, as people are being deprived of essential services due to absence of elected representatives in the grassroots bodies.
The EC plans to hold the elections to local government bodies in phases to ensure peaceful polls and avoid violence that marked many local elections in the past.
Since there are no elected representatives in almost all the local bodies, the commission estimates that it would take 10-12 months to complete the elections to all the bodies.
As part of preparation to conduct elections to local government bodies throughout the country, the commission is now revising separate rules and election codes for city corporations, municipalities, zila parishads, upazila parishads and union parishads. The move aims to modernise the rules and also align these with amended local government laws that restored non-partisan elections to the key posts (mayor and chairman) dropping the provision for the use of political party symbols.
The interim government amended the Local Government (Union Parishad) Act, 2009; Local Government (Municipality) Act, 2009; Upazila Parishad Act,1998; Zila Parishad Act, 2000; and Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009. The amendments were later ratified by Parliament.
“We want to complete the updating and reform of the rules and codes of conduct related to all types of local government elections by June next,” said Election Commissioner Abdur Rahmanel Masud.
Though separate rules and codes will remain for different local government bodies, the codes of conduct will be largely similar across all categories, he told UNB on Sunday.
The code of conduct for local government will also largely be similar to the code used for the February 12 parliamentary election, he added.
About the possible changes, the Election Commissioner said the use of posters will be banned, while stricter provisions will be incorporated to check misinformation and disinformation and misuse of AI particularly on social media.
The requirement for collecting signatures of a specific number of voters will be removed, while the amount of security deposit for candidates, except women contesting in reserved seats will be raised to rational level, he said.
The EC will publish draft rules on its website for at least 15 days to seek public opinions and suggestions from stakeholders, he said, adding that the Commission may also hold consultations with stakeholders on the proposed rules, although no final decision has yet been made.
About the possible timeframe for the elections, Rahmanel Masud said the period from late October to March next would be most suitable for the arrangement of elections.
Asked about the EC’s priority Rahmanel Masud: “We will suggest holding elections based on needs. In that case, elections to union parishads and municipalities should come first and elections to city corporations should be held at the last stage.”
When attention was drawn to local body elections marred by violence in the past, he said the current election commission, headed by AMM Nasir Uddin, would be very careful to make the upcoming elections free from violence like the 13th parliamentary election that was most peaceful.
“We’ll be very careful so that there are no casualties in local body elections. We’ll arrange the staggered elections to deploy a larger number of law enforcers in the election areas,” he said, stressing the need for cooperation from all stakeholders in maintaining a peaceful election environment.
The election commissioner said the EC would initially rely on regular law enforcement agencies, including police, RAB, BGB and Ansar, to maintain law and order during the elections. If necessary, the armed forces may be deployed later, he added.
According to EC estimates, elections to 12 city corporations (excluding newly formed Bogura city corporation), over 450 upazila parishads, more than 300 municipalities and 61 zila parishads are already overdue and can be held immediately without legal complications.
Besides, the legal timeframe for holding elections to around 600 union parishads began in April, making polls mandatory by October next. The 180-day countdown for elections in more than 2,800 additional union parishads will begin by July.
As the local body elections are arranged at the request from the local government division, the EC will announce election schedules after receiving a green signal from the government.

item.title: 3 suffer burn injuries at Bangshal shop fire
item.description:
Three workers suffered burn injuries when a fire broke out at a hardware shop in the city’s Bangshal area on Monday.
The injured were identified as Miraj, 25, Ifat, 20, and Rocky, 26.
Rafin, manager of the shop, said the fire broke out at shop on Tekerhat Lane around 11am as soon as an electric switch was turned on, leaving the three workers injured.
They were taken to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
Dr Shawon Bin Rahman, resident surgeon of the institute, said Ifat suffered burns on 25% of his body, while Rocky 23% and Miraj 2%.

item.title: 10 people pushed in by BSF remain stranded at Benapole border zero line
item.description:
Ten people, including women and children, allegedly pushed into Bangladesh by India's Border Security Force (BSF) through the Benapole border in Jessore's Sharsha upazila, are currently stranded at the border zero line.
The group has been staying at the Bombay Tala field in Sadipur village along the Benapole border since late Monday night, according to border authorities.
Sources at the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said the individuals were pushed into the Sadipur border area through a gate in the barbed-wire fence. Members of a patrol team from the Jessore 49 BGB Battalion intercepted them after learning of the incident and prevented them from entering further into Bangladesh.
Confirming the matter, Lt Col Golam Mohammad Saiful Alam Khan, commander of the Jessore 49 BGB Battalion, said the 10 individuals remain at the India-Bangladesh zero line in Sadipur.
"A letter has been sent to the BSF regarding the matter, and a flag meeting between the BGB and BSF has been scheduled for around 10am to resolve the issue," he said.

item.title: Govt offices, banks reopen as Eid-ul-Azha holiday ends
item.description:
Government offices, banks and courts across Bangladesh reopened on Monday after the end of a seven-day Eid-ul-Azha holiday.
Besides, many private-sector offices also resumed operations, prompting thousands of people to return to their workplaces in Dhaka and other cities after spending the holiday with their families.
Government, semi-government, autonomous, semi-autonomous and private offices remained closed from May 25 to May 31.
Many employees extended their vacations by taking additional leave beyond the official holiday period. As a result, a festive holiday atmosphere is likely to persist in many workplaces for the next couple of days.
Meanwhile, people from different parts of the country have started returning to their workplaces by road, rail and waterway after the Eid break.
Passenger and vehicle pressure has been gradually increasing at bus terminals, railway stations and launch terminals across the country.
A significant influx of returning passengers was observed at Kamalapur Railway Station in the capital on Sunday afternoon.

item.title: The Padma Barrage: Ignoring historical warnings
item.description:
Before the barrages, before the embankments, before the Krug Mission and the Flood Action Plan and the Ecnec approvals that now arrive every few decades bearing price tags in the billions -- before any of this, there was the bend.
The Kopai River carves a sharp turn through the Rarh region of western Bengal, a landscape of laterite soil that turns the water rust-red in monsoon. At this bend, which the novelist Tarashankar Bandyopadhyay would later make immortal under the name Hansuli Turn , the Kahar community lived out a relationship with the river that was not merely economic or hydrological but ritual.
The Kahars were an “untouchable” community whose traditional livelihood of palanquin-bearing had collapsed under modernity’s advance. They turned, as so many marginal communities in Bengal have always turned, to the river and the land it nourished. But their agriculture was not the simple matter of planting and harvest. It depended on an embankment -- one they maintained not as the state maintains infrastructure, with budgets and contractors and five-year plans, but as a community maintains a covenant.
The elders walked the bank at dawn, reading the water’s mood. When the monsoon came, they understood that the river must be allowed to spill -- not everywhere, not without guidance, but enough to deposit its gift of silt. This was flood not a disaster but as renewal, negotiated across generations.
Tarashankar’s 1947 novel Hansuli Banker Upakatha -- translated into English as The Tale of Hansuli Turn is built around a fundamental conflict. On one side stand Banwari and Suchand, the elders who maintain the community’s myths and their ritual relationship with the land. The river is understood as a living presence, named for Kopavati, a wrathful woman who can destroy everything during monsoon yet remains fertile with sediment and yields good crops.
On the other side stands Karali, a young Kahar who sees the old ways as chains. He brings railroads, wage labour, brick kilns. He breaks from the community’s stories. And in breaking from the stories, he severs the covenant. The embankment, no longer maintained as ritual, begins its slow decay. The river, no longer negotiated with, becomes an adversary.
Tarashankar was not writing environmental policy. He was writing fiction -- recognized as one of the great novels of modern Bengal. But what his novel captures with the precision that only literature can achieve is what was lost when river management was severed from community practice and handed to external authorities.
The Kahars’ embankment was never merely infrastructure. It was the physical manifestation of a social contract. When Karali chose the railroad over the ritual, he did not simply modernize. He broke a relationship that had sustained life at Hansuli Turn for longer than memory.
The knight and his doubt
What Tarashankar captured in fiction, a knighted British engineer had already spent his final years trying to tell the empire -- and being ignored.
Sir William Willcocks was born in India in 1852, trained at Roorkee Engineering College, and went on to design the first Aswan Dam, completed in 1902. He was knighted for his services to imperial irrigation. He designed the Hindiya Barrage on the Euphrates, bringing 3.5 million acres under cultivation in Mesopotamia.
This was, by any measure, one of the most accomplished civil engineers of the imperial age -- a man who had spent his entire career building precisely the kind of large-scale hydraulic infrastructure that defined colonial development and that the Padma Barrage, approved by Bangladesh’s Ecnec in May 2026, proposes to replicate at a Phase I cost of Tk 33,474 crore.
And yet.
In 1930, near the end of his life, the 78-year-old Willcocks stood before the University of Calcutta and delivered a series of lectures that amounted to an indictment of his own tradition. The lectures, published by the university under the title Lectures on the Ancient System of Irrigation in Bengal and Its Application to Modern Problems , argued that British rule had destroyed a superior indigenous irrigation system in Bengal.
Working alongside the malariologist CA Bentley, Willcocks contended that pre-colonial Bengal had possessed a system of “overflow irrigation” that was admirably suited both to agricultural productivity and to malaria control. The annual flooding that colonial engineers saw as a problem to be controlled was, in fact, the mechanism by which the delta renewed its fertility.
Silt-laden water, guided by community-maintained embankments and allowed to spill onto floodplains in controlled ways, deposited nutrients and raised land levels. Stagnant water bred mosquitoes; flowing, silt-heavy water did not.
The colonial administration had not improved Bengal’s waterscape. It had, Willcocks argued, wrecked it -- replacing a negotiated relationship with the delta’s dynamics with rigid embankments that separated land from water, reduced fertility, and increased disease.
The historian Daniel Klingensmith, in research presented to the American Historical Association in 2011, confirms that Willcocks and Bentley’s ideas “received widespread acceptance.” But the colonial administration could not accept them. To do so would have required admitting that its entire approach to water management in Bengal was not merely imperfect but actively destructive.
The knowledge was institutionally buried. The lectures were published -- a 128-page volume with a folded map, later reprinted in 1984 by BR Publishing Corporation in Delhi -- but the policy did not change. The embankments stayed.
Willcocks died two years after the lectures, in 1932, estranged from the establishment that had knighted him. His obituary in Nature described him as “fond of controversy” and “somewhat intolerant of adverse opinion” -- the language of institutional marginalization rendered as personality flaw -- but conceded that “subsequent events have vindicated many of his opinions.” He died on the margins, vindicated but uncelebrated.
The unbroken logic
What followed Willcocks’s warning was not a change of course but a deepening of the logic he had warned against.
In 1954 and 1955, devastating floods struck East Pakistan. The United Nations dispatched what became known as the Krug Mission, which recommended the “Cordon Approach” -- uninterrupted embankments separating floodplains from rivers. This was precisely the logic Willcocks had argued against.
A Dutch water engineering professor, Willem Johan van Blommenstein, served on the mission. The Dutch came from a delta that carries 2.7 million tons of sediment annually -- a landscape where the cordon approach made a certain sense.
The Bengal delta carries between 1.5 and 2 billion tons. They were solving a problem their rivers did not pose, using methods their landscape could sustain, and imposing them on a delta that works by entirely different rules.
From 1961 to 1964, the Coastal Embankment Project, funded by USAID and inspired by the Dutch polder system, constructed approximately 4,800 kilometres of embankments, creating 139 permanent polders.
The community practices that Willcocks had documented -- and that Tarashankar’s fictional Kahars had lived -- were declared obsolete. Within decades, riverbeds silted up. Land inside polders subsided below river level. Permanent waterlogging began affecting over two million people.
By the 1990s, Dutch experts were deeply involved in Bangladesh’s Flood Action Plan, and from 2012, Dutch-Bangladesh water cooperation officially shifted “from traditional aid to sustainable trade,” focusing on “economic cooperation, investment, and trade promotion.” The cordon approach persisted under new branding. The warning Willcocks had delivered in 1930 remained unheeded.
Then, in the 1990s, something remarkable happened in the southwest delta. Communities facing permanent waterlogging did what their ancestors would have done, though the knowledge had to be painfully reconstructed. They broke open a polder embankment.
The state sued them for destroying government property. But the tidal water rushed in, deposited sediment, raised the land -- and the waterlogging receded. Tidal River Management, the very system Willcocks had described in 1930, was rediscovered through an act of civil disobedience. It was later recognized in the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100, though it remains chronically underfunded.
And now, 2026 : The Padma Barrage has been approved. A 2.1-kilometre structure with 78 spillway gates, 18 undersluices, two fish passes, a navigation lock, and a railway bridge. Storage of 2,900 million cubic metres -- roughly 3 BCM -- on a river that carries between 350 and 525 BCM annually.
The promised irrigation for 1.9 million hectares would require, by the calculations of water expert Professor Md Khalequzzaman, between 9 and 26 BCM of water. The math does not work.
The sediment, estimated at 400 to 600 million tons annually, will be trapped. The delta will starve. The warnings Willcocks delivered in 1930 are being ignored again -- this time not by colonial administrators but by our own.
The man who became a myth
There is another figure in this story, one who lives where the failure of taming the river has already unfolded.
In Syed Mustafa Siraj’s Sahitya Akademi Award-winning novel Aleek Manush , set in Murshidabad district on the banks of the Padma, the protagonist Safi is a rebel who rejects the state, which he views as a “torture machine” run by complicit officers and state-owned “hooligans.”
The Farakka Barrage looms over this landscape -- the original wound, the structure that slashed dry-season flows and began the saline advance into the Sundarbans.
Safi, wandering the eroded banks, becomes a mythical figure to both Hindus and Muslims. The novel’s title, Aleek Manush , means “The Unreal Man” -- an irony the text itself insists upon, for Safi is very much flesh and blood, very much real. What is unreal, the novel suggests, is the state’s claim to legitimacy, its promise that structures like Farakka serve the people.
Siraj, who spent his youth traveling rural West Bengal with the folk theatre group Aalkaap, brought to his writing what the poet-journalist Syed Hasmat Jalal called “an unparalleled creative genius.”
The novelist Sunil Gangopadhyay observed that Siraj depicted rural Bengal “with far more authenticity than writers like me who live in the city.” And Siraj himself was explicit about his philosophical commitments: “I am free of religious belief,” he said, but also “tolerant towards anybody’s religion.”
His deeper conviction was that the state, particularly in its relationship with nature and rural communities, was a mechanism of violence. “Man tries to control nature,” he observed, “as for example building a dam across a river.”
The violence of not listening
There is a theoretical name for what has happened here.
The scholar Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, in her foundational essay “ Can the Subaltern Speak? ”, argued that marginalized communities are structurally silenced not because they lack voice, but because the very framework of institutional expertise renders their knowledge inaudible. The subaltern speaks. The powerful cannot hear -- not out of malice alone, but because the structure of power determines what counts as knowledge and whose knowledge counts.
This is the arc that connects Willcocks in 1930 to the Ecnec approval in 2026.
Willcocks, unusually for a colonial engineer -- perhaps uniquely for a knighted designer of the Aswan Dam -- tried to hear what the delta and its people were saying. He recognized that the overflow irrigation system was not primitive but sophisticated, not superstition but science of a different order. He was ignored. His ideas were institutionally buried.
The Krug Mission did not consult the communities whose irrigation systems they dismantled. The Dutch model was imposed without asking whether a low-sediment delta’s solutions could work in the most sediment-rich delta on earth. Tidal River Management emerged only because communities, facing inundation, forced it through direct action -- breaking the law to prove what the law had made unhearable.
And now the Padma Barrage is approved, with claims of irrigation, salinity reduction, and hydropower that the evidence does not support.
The promised irrigation would require three to nine times the water the barrage can store. The sediment trapping will replicate and compound the ecological damage Farakka has inflicted for half a century.
The promised benefits to fisheries ignore that hilsa migration, already disrupted by Farakka, will be obstructed further. No comprehensive, public Environmental Impact Assessment (EIS) has been conducted. The communities whose lives will be reshaped by this structure have not been meaningfully consulted.
The epistemological violence continues. Only the passports of the engineers have changed.
The question the river asked
Picture Sir William Willcocks in Calcutta, 1930.
He is 78 years old. He has built dams across the Nile and the Euphrates. He has been knighted by an empire. He has spent his career in the service of precisely the kind of large-scale hydraulic engineering that the Padma Barrage represents.
And he is standing in a university hall, at the end of his life, telling that empire that the Bengali peasants it dismissed as primitive understood the delta better than its finest engineers.
Willcocks died, estranged from the establishment he had served whose lectures were published, then ignored. The cordon approach rolled on through the Krug Mission, the Coastal Embankment Project, the Flood Action Plan. Farakka was built. The polders were built. The waterlogging came.
The TRM communities had to break the law to prove what Willcocks had told the university 70 years earlier. And now the Padma Barrage proposes to repeat the pattern on an even larger scale.
At Hansuli Turn , the brick kilns that Karali’s logic brought now line the Kopai’s banks. The river Tarashankar immortalized is reduced to a trickle. The embankment the Kahars maintained as ritual has been replaced by an embankment the state built and abandoned. The covenant is broken.
At Murshidabad, on the banks of the Padma, Safi still walks. The Aleek Manush . The unreal man who is more real than the state’s promises. He walks where Farakka’s downstream consequences continue to unfold -- the erosion, the water scarcity, the slow saline creep. He is a figure of resistance against the very logic that now proposes to build another barrage, further downstream, with the same justifications and the same silences.
And Sir William Willcocks, the knight who listened when his empire would not, asks from 1930 the question that has never been answered, only deferred: Will we learn to negotiate with the river, or will we keep building monuments until the delta can bear no more?
The river told him. He tried to tell us. The question remains, and the Ganges Treaty expires in December. The decision window is open. For now.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. His email address is zakir.kibria@gmail.com

item.title: Brazil thrash Panama 6-2 in World Cup send-off
item.description:
Brazil turned on the style with a 6-2 drubbing of Panama on Sunday in a lopsided World Cup send-off at the Maracana Stadium in Rio de Janeiro.
Real Madrid star Vinicius Jr fired the Brazilians into the lead inside the opening minute, collecting a pass from veteran midfielder Casemiro before lashing in a thunderous strike from 25 yards.
The five-time World Cup-winners were jolted though in the 14th minute when Panama grabbed a freak equaliser, Michael Murillo's free-kick taking a wicked deflection off Matheus Cunha and sailing past Brazil keeper Alisson.
The combination of Vinicius and Casemiro restored Brazil's advantage six minutes before half-time.
Vinicius jinked into space on the left hand side of the penalty area, and what looked like a curling shot destined for the far corner was helped into the net by a glancing header from Casemiro.
Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti rang the changes at half-time, replacing his entire starting line-up with the exception of Leo Pereira as the second half got under way.
The new-look Selecao wasted no time in asserting their superiority, rattling in three quick goals to put Brazil 5-1 up.
Teenager Rayan made it 3-1 in the 53rd minute, the 19-year-old Bournemouth talent collecting a misplaced pass from Panama goalkeeper Orlando Mosquera on the right flank and calmly curling in his shot to the delight of the Maracana crowd.
Lucas Paqueta swept in Brazil's fourth from the edge of the area in the 60th minute, and Igor Thiago made it 5-1 from the penalty spot three minutes later after being brought down by Mosquera.
Botafogo's Danilo completed Brazil's scoring in the 81st minute, controlling Paqueta's floated pass into the box before wrongfooting the covering Panama defence and burying the finish.
Panama grabbed a late consolation when Carlos Harvey crashed in a 30-yard screamer.
Brazil face a final friendly against Egypt in Cleveland, Ohio next Saturday, before opening their World Cup Group C campaign against Morocco on June 13.
The Brazilians also face Haiti and Scotland in the first round of the tournament.

item.title: 11,613 Bangladeshi Hajj pilgrims return home
item.description:
A total of 11,613 Bangladeshi Hajj pilgrims have returned home from Saudi Arabia as of Sunday, following the completion of this year's Hajj held on June 26.
"A total of 28 return flights were operated by three designated carriers -- one by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, one by Saudia Airlines and two by Flynas Airlines," an official familiar with the development said here.
Hajj office said so far, 1,253 Hajis returned under government management, while 10,360 under private travel agencies arrangements in 28 flights -six by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, eight by Saudia Airlines, and 14 by Flynas Airlines.
"We expect that 5,698 Hajis will return Monday by 14 flights while 3,254 will come Tuesday with eight flights, " he said.
According to the flight schedule, 4,513 Hajis will return back on June 3 by 11 flights, 3,248 will come with eight flights on June 4 and 2,925 Hajis are set to return on June 5 by seven flights.
At least 41 Bangladeshi pilgrims have passed away in Saudi Arabia during Hajj with 27 males and 14 females. Of them, 30 died in Makkah and 11 in Madinah.
No deaths have been reported in Jeddah, Mina, or Muzdalifah.
This year's Hajj operations began with the first outbound flight on April 18 and concluded on May 21.
The return Hajj flights started on May 30 and will continue until June 30.

item.title: Rethinking development storytelling
item.description:
There is an uncomfortable truth that both the development sector and the entertainment industry in Bangladesh have long avoided confronting openly.
For years, development organizations have invested heavily in documentaries, awareness videos, campaign films, and advocacy content. Many are sincere, technically strong, and socially important, yet most remain confined to workshops, donor reports, institutional platforms, or social media feeds where audiences quickly move on.
They often meet organizational objectives but rarely become part of the wider public. Meanwhile, mainstream cinema and OTT platforms continue focusing largely on romance, crime, thrillers, and urban stories, while the realities of climate frontlines, labour communities, migration, and marginalized lives rarely enter mainstream entertainment with commercial ambition or emotional depth.
Between these two worlds, development storytelling and mainstream entertainment, a quiet wall of misunderstanding has existed for years.
One myth inside the development sector suggests that audiences do not want to engage with stories of marginalized communities unless they are framed as “awareness content.” Another myth within parts of the entertainment industry assumes that films connected to advocacy or development themes inevitably lose commercial appeal and audience engagement.
Cha Gorom , a film by Shankha Dasgupta, co-created by Oxfam and Chorki with support from the European Union, challenged both myths.
Approximately a year and a half ago, Cha Gorom was not even a title but a restless idea and a question that kept disturbing me: Why are Bangladesh’s tea gardens always shown only from the outside?
For decades, films, advertisements, and tourism campaigns have celebrated their beauty yet rarely explored the emotional world of the people who sustain that industry. Over the years, I increasingly felt development storytelling needed a new language. We did not need another documentary that simply informed audiences but rather a commercially viable, emotionally engaging story.
That dream of going out of our zone eventually became the beginning of Cha Gorom . The journey was long and uncertain. We started with research, field visits, discussions, and endless conversations across Dhaka and Sylhet. Oxfam's leadership and the European Union's support encouraged the vision. Gradually, people began joining the journey: Redoan Rony, Jabed Sultan Pias, Masudul Amin Rintu, director Shankha Dasgupta, writer Saifullah Riyad, actors, actress, and eventually the entire cast and crew.
One of the most important turning points was shaping the storytelling approach. Saifullah Riyad understood early that the tea garden could not simply become a backdrop of suffering. From Oxfam, we provided all aspects -- research, community access, history, culture, lived realities, and multiple story angles, while consciously ensuring creative freedom for the filmmakers. Director Shankha Dasgupta then translated those realities beautifully onto the screen.
What audiences connected with most deeply in Cha Gorom was its humanity. Safa Kabir’s portrayal of Irene, a young doctor entering an unfamiliar social world, brought emotional vulnerability, curiosity, and empathy into the narrative. Through Irene, viewers gradually entered a tea garden reality they often overlook in everyday life.
Sarah Jabin Aditi’s Nandini carried a quiet emotional intensity that reflected the layered psychological realities of marginalized women without falling into melodrama. At the same time, Rezwan Pervez’s Robin Chand Murmu emerged as one of the film’s discoveries, bringing grounded realism, philosophy of life, emotional depth, and authenticity to the story. Mithu, played by Partho Sheikh, is charming, flawed, careless, philosophical, and deeply human.
Many viewers later wrote that these characters felt like people they personally knew. That is the true power of emotionally intelligent storytelling.
After its release, social media and mainstream media reactions became revealing. Some viewers appreciated the natural performances. Others highlighted the emotional simplicity of the storytelling.
Journalists, writers, celebrities, masses of people, and cultural commentators wrote positively about how the film balanced entertainment and realism without becoming preachy. Many ordinary viewers mentioned how the film made them rethink tea garden communities for the first time. Many appreciated the approach of Oxfam in the film production.
One viewer wrote something that stayed with me deeply: “This film did not make tea workers look helpless. It made them look human.” That sentence perhaps summarizes the real achievement of the movie. Because dignity matters in storytelling.
Marginalized people should not always appear only as victims waiting to be saved. They laugh, joke, love, dream, flirt, become frustrated, make mistakes, and carry emotional complexity like everyone else. And this is where the development of storytelling must evolve.
The future of advocacy communication cannot remain trapped inside expensive documentary models that only circulate within development circles. If social storytelling wants mass impact, it must learn the language of entertainment, emotion, and popular culture.
The development sector should not automatically view commercialization as the enemy of social impact. In fact, Cha Gorom proved the opposite with stories and further engagements with Robi and Revital Tea.
When audiences voluntarily spend Pohela Boishakh watching a film rooted in tea garden realities, advocacy has already entered public consciousness, living rooms, in a much more profound way than many traditional campaigns achieve.
For me, Cha Gorom journey also revealed another important lesson for Bangladesh’s creative industry. Development organizations should not be treated merely as sponsors or funding sources.
Organizations like Oxfam contribute far beyond money, including knowledge, field access, research, community trust, social understanding, advocacy insight, and human stories that mainstream cinema often cannot access authentically.
Similarly, NGOs must also learn to trust storytelling itself rather than trying to dominate narratives through excessive development and branding anxiety. Audiences do not emotionally connect with logos. They connect with truth, characters, emotion, and humanity.
In Bangladesh there are countless untold stories across climate change, migration, labour, gender, rivers, urbanization, and marginalized communities that can become mainstream cinema if treated with emotional honesty and cinematic intelligence.
Perhaps the real future lies in a new collaborative model where OTT platforms, filmmakers, writers, artists, communities, and development organizations work together.
Personally, Cha Gorom remains one of the most emotional journeys of my life. It has been about breaking a mindset: Breaking the myth that development storytelling cannot be entertaining, breaking the myth that socially meaningful cinema cannot be commercially viable, and breaking the myth that audiences do not care about marginalized communities, and perhaps most importantly, breaking the myth that social impact and mainstream entertainment cannot walk together.
They can. And Cha Gorom has proved it.
Md Sariful Islam is Head of Influencing, Communications, Advocacy and Media, Oxfam in Bangladesh.

item.title: An ode to reforms
item.description:
“To serve or not to serve -- that is the question.
“Whether it’s our karma to witness rape and murder/ Or that the citizens look resigned to bribery and extortion/ The mafia are protected, the honest deserve injustice/ The youth’s dreams of jobs fade/ Are taxpayers bound to pay for inflated projects, suffer power outage?/ Shall depositors get back bank money? And how to raise voice again to bring change/ For the reforms promised miss action and diction/ Thus the masses quietly bear anger/ Then who are there to stand up for the powerless?”
This is a parody inspired by the soliloquy "To be, or not to be, that is the question" in William Shakespeare's Hamlet . The parody covers some of the current Bangladesh issues that are affecting people's life or creating resentment among the conscious segment.
Before the rape and murder of eight-year-old Ramisa in May, there was already a 35% rise in such crimes in April compared to the previous month. The law enforcement personnel had to remain busy dealing with quite a number of extortion cases recently.
Against this backdrop, the government of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) has spelt out some development pledges, crafted with jargons in the official 8th five-year plan, that were part of the party's pre-election manifesto to woo the voters.
Creation of 10 million jobs by 2030, turning Bangladesh into a $1 trillion economy by 2034, transformation of agriculture into a high-value sector, increasing investment in public and private sectors, widening export base, higher revenue mobilization, and raising the budget to improve quality of education and healthcare services are some of the major pledges in addition to the critical ones to rebuild systems and institutions.
Attractive, interesting, and timely, albeit ambitious. Yet, these are just promises on paper unless or until they are translated into new reality -- our record of execution of pre-poll pledges is not the best.
Now dealing with the unforeseen reality, will you focus only on addressing the evolving issues you are struggling with to pacify your critics, or concentrate on delivering services as per the manifesto, ignoring the contemporary issues?
In any case or in the pursuit of both the objectives simultaneously, the government needs to prove political willingness and acumen, capacity, determination, due diligence and prudence if it really means business in the delivery of public service.
Furthermore, in the age of social media, people no longer believe in some kind of “steps to be taken” approach. They want to know exactly what you have done or at least how the job would be accomplished.
In an objective scenario, any proponent of democracy would admit that the implementation of what the BNP as a political party promised the people before and after the fall of fascist Hasina regime, especially prior to the parliamentary polls, is simply not possible if the culture of governing the country remains the same.
In the meantime, public expectations and demographic distribution in the political landscape have quietly changed, as exposed slightly during and in the aftermath of the July-August 2024 revolution. Obviously, the state machinery with anti-people orientation and the baggage of about two decades would serve all but benevolent forces and the greater population, who took to the streets in 2024 and elected their representatives from whatever options were available in 2026.
That is the key challenge for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman because his elected regime has been assigned to set in motion democratic governance. Not to go ahead with Hasina's oligarchical rule, but to uphold national interest and ensure maximum public welfare.
A mere soft-spoken image and sincere wish of the incumbent head of the government won't bear fruit if he doesn't have a competent and dedicated team to materialize his words. Well-coordinated teamwork too may not produce the desired results unless the government's legal instruments and institutions work properly.
Unfortunately, the recent rise in incidents of rape, killing, and other forms of crimes and violence demonstrates fearless behaviour of criminals. Any leader would want to improve law and order but to do so, you have to deliver justice and end the culture of impunity. Is it possible to attain overnight what had not been possible without judicial reform, which has been neglected by allowing the executive to interfere with the judiciary?
You cannot guarantee either the citizens' rights or security by giving any signal that bureaucrats, law enforcers, and the men of defense establishment are above law. So, the National Human Rights Commission, if empowered, can excuse the political regime from undue responsibility of dealing with such sensitive issues.
When you've felt it is necessary to create millions of jobs, attain a double-digit gross domestic product (GDP) growth, increase investment manifold, and restore public confidence in banks by reviving them, it is imperative to carry out economic reforms. That is essential for smooth functioning of the economic lifeblood of every stakeholder in society, except plunderers of public resources.
If you are really serious about ending official corruption, bribery, commissions, tender manipulation, and abuse of power in broad daylight, there is no alternative to autonomous functioning of institutions such as a Anti-Corruption Commission.
We also need the media to be liberated from the clutches of external forces so that they may operate to serve public interests and ensure transparency and accountability of the authorities.
Any elected government in developing countries like ours is criticized for deficiency in the so-called good governance, although what we need is fair and equitable management in running the state. The people's representatives will not be able to deliver democratic, welfare-oriented governance as long as they are sabotaged by vested quarters. Hence, massive regulatory reforms are the only option.
A new democratic culture, as people had envisioned throughout the anti-fascist movements, shall not evolve unless we carry out political reforms and the politicians change their mindset. Otherwise, the political parties and politicians in parliament today may also face an existential crisis soon.
These political parties -- the ruling BNP, and opposition Jamaat-e-Islami, and National Citizens' Party (NCP) -- have a historic responsibility to work together for implementing the reforms they agreed upon earlier to build the foundation for uninterrupted democratic governance in the country.
Whether "to be or not to be" is a matter of their political choice.
Khawaza Main Uddin is a journalist. He can be reached at khawaza@gmail.com . Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Couple found dead in Chittagong hotel
item.description:
A couple was found dead at a hotel in Foy’s Lake area of the Chittagong port city on Monday.
The deceased were identified as Mohamamd Ripon and Sonia.
They checked into Royel's Park Hotel on Sunday night identifying themselves as a married couple.
Kamruzzaman, Officer-in-Charge of Akbarshah Police Station, said getting no response from the room of the couple, the hotel authorities informed the matter to police who recovered the bodies around 11am.
However, efforts are underway to know their detailed addresses, he said.
“It is still unclear how the couple died. However, an investigation is ongoing to unearth the mystery behind the incident,” said OC Kamruzzaman.
The bodies were taken to Chittagong Medical College and Hospital morgue for autopsy.

item.title: Teen-X founder Shahi Al Sadat, 17, leads fight against teenage rape in Bangladesh
item.description:
Seventeen-year-old Shahi Al Sadat, a student of St. Joseph Higher Secondary School, has emerged as a prominent youth activist dedicated to protecting teenagers from rape, trafficking, harassment, and online exploitation.
Through Teen-X, a technology-driven support platform founded on 2 June 2021, Sadat has been leading awareness campaigns, advocacy efforts, and victim-support initiatives aimed at creating a safer environment for young people.
Founded with the vision of creating a safer environment for young people, Teen-X has grown into a platform that provides awareness, support, guidance, and advocacy for victims of abuse and exploitation.
Over the years, the initiative has conducted campaigns, workshops, and community-based programs focused on preventing violence against teenagers and promoting child rights.
One of Teen-X’s most significant achievements came through its assistance in multiple victim-support and awareness efforts that contributed to the arrest of seven accused rapists, highlighting the platform’s role in supporting justice and empowering survivors to seek help.
Sadat’s leadership and impact have earned him widespread recognition on both national and international stages.
In 2024, he became the Winner of the National Tech Award, recognizing his contribution to technology-driven social impact and youth innovation.
His growing list of achievements continued in 2025, when he received the PBIF International Business Award 2025, the 71 Media Iconic Award 2025, the Star Bangladesh Award 2025, the South Asian Excellence Award 2025, and the Global Excellence Award 2025 for his outstanding work in child protection, digital advocacy, and youth leadership.
Adding to these accomplishments, Sadat was honored with the Global Iconic Award 2026, further strengthening his reputation as a young changemaker from Bangladesh whose initiatives are creating measurable social impact.
Teen-X also achieved international recognition in 2026, when Team Teen-X won the Gold Medal at the WICE 2026 National Round Bangladesh, marking another milestone for the youth-led organization and showcasing its innovation on a competitive platform.
In addition to these recognitions, Sadat was nominated for the International Children’s Peace Prize 2024, one of the world’s most prestigious honors for young changemakers, for his contributions to child rights, digital safety, and youth empowerment.
Through Teen-X and several youth-focused initiatives, Sadat has reached thousands of students with awareness campaigns on cyber safety, child protection, anti-harassment education, and legal support.
His work continues to inspire young people across Bangladesh to use technology, leadership, and social innovation as tools for change.
“Every teenager deserves safety, dignity, and the opportunity to live without fear,” Sadat said while speaking about the mission behind Teen-X.
As Bangladesh continues its fight against gender-based violence and child exploitation, the efforts of young leaders like Shahi Al Sadat demonstrate how youth-driven innovation and community action can play a powerful role in building a safer future for the next generation.

item.title: Mahrez leads as Zidane’s son included in Algeria World Cup squad
item.description:
Vladimir Petkovic has named his 26-man squad for the FIFA World Cup 2026, where Algeria will take on holders Argentina, Austria and Jordan in Group J.
Captain Riyad Mahrez and record appearance-maker Aissa Mandi are among the the team's most experienced squad members, alongside midfielder Nabil Bentaleb, who returns after an injury-disrupted international career.
Goalkeeper Luca Zidane, son of 1998 World Cup winner Zinedine Zidane, also makes the grade despite suffering a broken chin and jaw while playing for Granada in April. The 28-year-old has won six caps since debuting for Les Fennecs last October, with Oussama Benbot and Melvin Mastil completing the goalkeeping trio.
In another boost for Petkovic, attacking duo Houssem Aouar and Amine Gouiri are back in the fold after missing the Africa Cup of Nations through injury.
Algeria, who are playing at their first World Cup since losing in the Round of 16 to eventual winners Germany at Brazil 2014, will play warm-up games against the Netherlands (3 June) and Bolivia (10 June), before beginning their Group J campaign against Argentina in Kansas City on 16 June.

item.title: Dooley hails Bangladesh's football passion ahead of first assignment
item.description:
Bangladesh national football team's newly appointed head coach, Thomas Dooley, has praised the country's unwavering passion for football, saying the extraordinary attention surrounding an upcoming friendly against San Marino reflects how deeply the sport is embedded in the nation's culture.
The German-American coach shared his thoughts on Facebook before Bangladesh's departure for Europe on Sunday, where the team will face San Marino in an international friendly on June 5. The match will mark Dooley's first outing since taking charge of the national side.
Despite spending only a few days in Dhaka and overseeing three training sessions, the 64-year-old said he has been struck by the extraordinary level of enthusiasm surrounding football in the country.
"As we leave for Europe for our upcoming test match, I continue to be amazed by the passion for football in Bangladesh," Dooley wrote.
The coach highlighted the remarkable attention the team has received despite the fixture being a friendly rather than a major tournament or qualifier.
"This is not a World Cup qualifier. It is not a continental championship. It is not even a match against a higher-ranked opponent. It is simply a friendly test game against a team ranked below us," he said.
"Yet the media attention has been extraordinary. Cameras lined both sides of the field. Reporters everywhere. Fans following every step."
According to Dooley, the overwhelming interest reflects the importance of football in Bangladesh and the expectations carried by the national team.
"That level of interest says everything about how much this country loves football. The expectations, the passion, and the support are immense. It is a privilege for me, our staff and players to represent millions of people who care so deeply about the game," he added.
The former United States international concluded his message by paying tribute to the country's football culture.
"Bangladesh football has a powerful heartbeat, and you can feel it every single day."
Bangladesh left Dhaka on Sunday for San Marino, where they will continue preparations with four more training sessions before Thursday's friendly.
Midfielder Hamza Choudhury, along with Shamit Shome and Zayyan Ahmed, are expected to join the squad in San Marino ahead of the match.

item.title: Ochoa set for record sixth World Cup as Mexico unveil 2026 squad
item.description:
Mexico have named veteran goalkeeper Guillermo Ochoa in their 26-man squad for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, making him the first Mexican player to be selected for six World Cup tournaments.
Head coach Javier Aguirre announced his squad on Sunday, a day after El Tri secured a 1-0 victory over Australia in a World Cup warm-up match, as the co-host nation prepares for the biggest tournament in its football history.
The inclusion of 40-year-old Ochoa is the headline decision in Aguirre's squad. The experienced goalkeeper, who made his World Cup debut in 2006, will now participate in a record sixth global finals after also being part of Mexico's squads in 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022.
At the opposite end of the spectrum is teenage sensation Gilberto Mora, who is set to become the youngest Mexican player ever to feature at a World Cup. The highly rated midfielder is just 17 years old and represents the future of Mexican football.
Aguirre, who is preparing for his third World Cup as Mexico coach after leading the team at the 2002 and 2010 editions, has blended youth with experience in a squad tasked with delivering a memorable campaign on home soil.
Mexico's best World Cup performances came when they hosted the tournament in 1970 and 1986, reaching the quarter-finals on both occasions. Aguirre will be aiming to match or better that achievement when the competition kicks off next year.
The squad retains a strong core from the team that played at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, with 12 players from that campaign earning selection once again.
Domestic giants Chivas are the most heavily represented club in the squad, contributing seven players despite operating exclusively with Mexican footballers.
As one of the three co-hosts alongside the United States and Canada, Mexico will enter the tournament carrying heightened expectations, with Aguirre hoping the experience of veterans such as Ochoa and the emergence of talents like Mora can inspire a deep run in front of home supporters.

item.title: Nepal opener joins exclusive club by hitting six sixes in an over
item.description:
Nepal batter Kushal Bhurtel joined an exclusive club of just six players when he smashed six sixes in an over during his side's T20I match against China on Sunday.
Bhurtel completed the feat in the ninth over of the contest at the Singapore National Cricket Ground in the opening match of the Asian Games Qualifier, when he launched left-arm spinner Chen Zhuo Yue over the rope a total of six times in succession across six legal deliveries.
It means Bhurtel becomes the second player from Nepal to have scored six sixes in an over in a T20I, with the right-hander joining Dipendra Singh Airee in an exclusive club of just six players to have recorded the milestone.
India great Yuvraj Singh was the first player to hit six sixes in an over when he launched England's Stuart Broad into the stands at the inaugural ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2007, while Bhurtel now joins West Indies hard-hitter Kieron Pollard (2021), Singh Airee (2024), Samoa's Darius Visser (2024) and Bulgaria's Manan Bashir (2025) in achieving the feat in T20I cricket.
Bhurtel ended the match with a superb innings of 129 from just 43 deliveries as Nepal went on to score 313/2 from their 20 overs, before they went on to record a comfortable 221-run victory.

Shopping malls, markets to remain open until 7pm
item.description:
The government has decided to restore the previous schedule for shopping malls, markets and shops, allowing them to remain open until 7pm from Tuesday as part of its electricity-saving measures.

At the same time, instructions have been issued to switch off all billboard lights and to ensure that ongoing and upcoming fairs, trade fairs and cultural programmes are concluded by 7pm.

The information was issued in a directive from the Coordination-2 Branch of the Power Division today, Monday.

Following instructions from the Prime Minister, shopping malls, markets and shops were allowed to remain open until 7pm and billboard lighting as well as various fairs, trade fairs and cultural events were required to be shut down by the same time as per to the previous schedule, the order reads.

However, on the occasion of the holy Eid-ul-Azha, shopping malls, markets and shops were temporarily allowed to remain open until 10 pm.

item.title: BSF attempts to ‘push in’ 13, including women and children, through Jashore border
item.description:
India’s Border Security Force (BSF) has attempted to push 13 people, including women and children, into Bangladesh through the Sadipur border in Sharsha upazila of Jashore.

However, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said the group was unable to enter the country due to heightened vigilance along the frontier.

The 13 individuals are currently stranded in the no-man’s-land between Bangladesh and India. Neither country has allowed them to cross the border. As of Monday evening, they were seen remaining under the open sky in the border area.

A flag meeting at deputy commander level between the BGB and BSF was held at the Sadipur border on Monday evening following the incident.

Lieutenant Colonel Saiful Alam Khan, commanding officer of the Jashore-49 BGB Battalion, told Prothom Alo, “The BSF attempted to push at least 13 people into Bangladesh last night. We will not allow them to enter Bangladesh. We made our firm position clear during the flag meeting.”

He added, “We have informed the BSF that if they are Bangladeshi citizens, they should be sent through the proper state-to-state process, in which case we will accept them. Otherwise, we will not tolerate attempts to push them across the border illegally. We will not allow anyone to cross Bangladesh’s zero line unlawfully.”

According to BGB sources, the BSF opened a gate in the border fence in the Jayantipur border area of India’s North 24 Parganas district on Sunday night and attempted to send several women, men and children into Bangladesh. They were gathered near the Sadipur border area along the Benapole frontier.

Sensing the move, a BGB patrol team that had already been on alert quickly reached the spot and foiled the attempt.

item.title: Curiosity sparks over ‘autonomous underwater vehicle’ caught in fishermen’s net in Bay
item.description:
A mechanical object, closely resembling an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV), has been caught in the nets of fishermen during a fishing expedition off the coast of Patharghata in Barguna.

The recovery of the red and yellow device, measuring approximately eight feet in length, has ignited widespread curiosity ranging from the local fishing community to administrative and research circles.

Oceanographers initially suspect that the object could be an ‘Autonomous Underwater Vehicle’ (AUV)—an automated subsurface research vessel.

Across the globe, such vessels are deployed for marine research, environmental monitoring, seabed mapping, climate data collection, and military surveillance.

Its appearance in the coastal waters of Bangladesh within the Bay of Bengal has raised significant interest.

‘We hauled in the net to find a machine, not fish’

Speaking to local fishermen, it was learned that on Sunday afternoon, a fishing trawler from the Khalifar Hat area of Charduani Union under Patharghata Upazila was fishing in the estuary area of the Bay of Bengal. While hauling in the net, the fishermen felt an unusual weight.

Miraj Hossain, a fisherman aboard the trawler, said, “Initially, we thought a large sailfish had been trapped in the net. But when we hauled it in, we saw it wasn’t a fish, but a machine. We have never seen anything like this before.”

Miraj added that upon noticing fin-like structures on the body of the device and various electronic gadgets inside, they grew somewhat panicked.

At first, many mistook it for a missile component or a military object. The fishermen subsequently lifted it onto the trawler, brought it to Patharghata on Monday morning, and notified the Patharghata police station. The Patharghata police station has since taken custody of the device.

What was observed on the device

Photographs of the recovered device show it to be a long, cylindrical, torpedo-shaped object. Both ends are rounded, and the rear section features fans or fins for stability. When the upper section is opened, various electronic modules, battery units, sensors, control systems, and an antenna-like communication device are visible inside.

To ascertain more about the object, photographs were sent to Professor Mohammad Abdul Aziz of the Department of Zoology at Jahangirnagar University, a renowned national expert on dolphins and marine zoology.

After examining the images, he told Prothom Alo, “Based on preliminary observations, I believe this could be an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle or AUV. I am unaware of any regular deployment of such vessels within our maritime boundaries. However, judging by the photos, it does not appear to have been operational. It is highly probable that it drifted towards the coast due to tidal currents after experiencing a mechanical failure or running out of power.”

Professor Abdul Aziz explained that these vessels typically remain underwater for extended periods to collect data autonomously before returning to a designated location or transmitting the data.

Experts noted that universities, research institutions, meteorological agencies, navies, and offshore oil and gas companies worldwide routinely utilise this technology.

Professor Abdul Aziz added, “I have no information regarding the use of such vessels in our country. If it belongs to another nation, the vessel may have drifted into our territorial waters after becoming non-functional.”

Technical analysis required

According to researchers, identifying the true nature of the device requires a thorough technical analysis of its serial number, manufacturer’s name, memory data, sensor configuration, and communication systems.

According to them, if the internal data remains intact, it could provide insights into its origin, how long it had been at sea, and the type of data it was gathering.

Mohammad Sohan, Sub-Inspector (SI) of Patharghata police station, stated that they took custody of the device after being alerted via the 999 emergency hotline. Contact is being established with relevant authorities and experts to determine the nature of the technology and its origin.

Tapas Paul, Patharghata Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO), said, “The matter is being treated with utmost seriousness. Further action will be taken based on expert opinions.”

Mir Mohammad Ali, Assistant Professor of the Department of Aquaculture at Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University and a marine life researcher, told Prothom Alo that if this truly is an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV), the public recovery of such a technological device on the coast of Bangladesh is quite rare.

The incident raises new questions regarding international marine research, climate monitoring, maritime resource exploration, and regional maritime security operations being conducted in the Bay of Bengal, he pointed out.

Uncovering its true identity through technical analysis could yield invaluable data concerning marine research and maritime management, he stated.

item.title: CHT Affairs Minister’s sudden resignation stirs discussions; what leaders-activists say
item.description:
The resignation of Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) Affairs Minister Dipen Dewan just three and a half months into the government's tenure has become a major topic of discussion in hill politics.

Leaders and activists involved in Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) politics, as well as members of the community in the hills, are trying to understand why Dipen Dewan made such a decision.

His followers staged a road blockade and protest in Rangamati demanding the withdrawal of his resignation and his reinstatement.

The protesters claim that Dipen Dewan was forced to resign due to pressure. However, in his resignation letter, he cited physical complications and illness.

Citing health issues, Dipen Dewan submitted his resignation letter to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today, Monday. Dipen Dewan, who had left a career as a joint district judge, contested a parliamentary election for the first time and was elected a member of parliament. He secured the largest margin of victory in the 13th parliamentary election.

After the BNP formed the government, Dipen Dewan was appointed Minister for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs. His father, Subimal Dewan, was an adviser on tribal affairs to the late President Ziaur Rahman. The State Minister for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs is Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin, MP from Chattogram-5 (Hathazari). He also serves as State Minister for Land.

Local BNP leaders said they had not anticipated Dipen Dewan’s resignation. They believe he may have resigned due to issues related to running the ministry, controlling Rangamati politics, and the process of appointing administrators to the district councils in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. However, no comment from Dipen Dewan was available.

The activities of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs Ministry are centred on the three hill districts. There are three parliamentary constituencies there. BNP candidates won all three seats in Rangamati, Khagrachhari, and Bandarban in the national election. Sa Ching Prue Jerry was elected from Bandarban and Wadud Bhuiyan from Khagrachhari.

At least six leaders associated with BNP politics in the CHT told Prothom Alo that although there had been disagreements among MPs from the hill constituencies on various issues in the past, the situation was different this time. Since all three MPs belong to the same party, cordial relations existed among them.

Minister for the Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs Dipen Dewan resigns

For various reasons, the CHT is an extremely sensitive region. Different ethnic communities live there, and in some cases there is a lack of mutual trust.

They said that after becoming minister, Dipen Dewan began working to improve the situation through discussions with public representatives and civil society.

On 11 May, CHT Affairs Minister Dipen Dewan visited Khagrachhari district. That afternoon he exchanged views with administrative officials and members of civil society at the Khagrachhari Circuit House. However, local MP Wadud Bhuiyan was not present at that meeting.

After Dipen Dewan’s resignation, Wadud Bhuiyan told Prothom Alo that he did not know the reason for the resignation. He said he had not attended the meeting that day due to illness. He added that he has a very good relationship with Dipen Dewan.

Local sources say that BNP politics had been divided over party nominations in this election, although the divisions remained hidden during the election period. They have now started to reappear openly. One side consists of Dipen Dewan’s followers, while the other consists of followers of district BNP president Dipon Talukder.

Dipon Talukder rejected the suggestion of party conflict. Speaking to Prothom Alo over the phone this afternoon, Monday, he said, “I know nothing about the minister’s (Dipen Dewan’s) resignation. I do not know why he resigned. This is entirely his personal matter. I did not receive any prior indication either.”

Saiful Islam Bhutto, vice-president of Rangamati district BNP, told Prothom Alo, “Dipen Dewan’s resignation is harmful to BNP politics, hill politics, and the formation of a ‘rainbow nation’ among all hill and Bengali communities. It will cause significant damage to the implementation of BNP’s 31-point state reform framework and 19-point programme. I urge the prime minister to take appropriate measures and return Dipen Dewan to the Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs Ministry.”

BNP leader Saiful Islam Bhutto further said, “Dipen Dewan is not physically ill. I have travelled with him in remote areas for a long time and have never seen him weak or sick. Some BNP leaders are trying to create instability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts by misleading the prime minister with false information.”

Sajamong Marma, senior vice-president of Kaukhali upazila BNP and an executive member of district BNP, said, “The reason he mentioned in the resignation letter is not correct. Physically and mentally he is capable of carrying out ministerial duties. Those who nurtured the fascist Awami League after 5 August pressured him into temporarily submitting his resignation letter.”

The Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs Ministry began its journey on 15 July 1998. It was established under the terms of the accord signed the previous year between the government and the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti. The objective of that accord was to restore peace in the hills after years of conflict.

The Chittagong Hill Tracts Accord contains 72 clauses divided into sections A, B, C and D. Most of them relate to the formation of district councils and the regional council. Clause 19 of section D provides for the establishment of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs Ministry. The clause states: “A ministry for Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs shall be established by appointing a minister from among the tribal people.”

Among the three members of parliament from the Chittagong Hill Tracts, two belong to hill communities and one is Bengali. Apart from Dipen Dewan, the other hill-community MP is Bandarban’s Sa Ching Prue Jerry.
